findings.claim: Every chapter foregrounds choices that managers, auditors, and external stakeholders must make under uncertainty, rather than algorithmic procedures with single right answers.
findings.failure_mode: overgeneralisation about the whole book
findings.evidence: Deep 17 frames the accounting cycle (Chs 3-5) as the 'disciplined backbone'; deep 102, 121 ('Cash will never be in an adjusting entry' [V]), 141-146 (four closing entries), 250-252 (petty cash, bank reconciliation) are procedural content with single right answers. No deep passage says every chapter foregrounds choice.
findings.fix: correct: Many chapters foreground choices that managers, auditors, and external stakeholders make under uncertainty (method selection, estimation, disclosure), sitting on top of the procedural accounting cycle.

findings.claim: revenue-recognition cutoff (HealthSouth in Ch 8.7)
findings.failure_mode: case attached to the wrong fraud mechanism
findings.evidence: Deep 256: HealthSouth used 'a combination of false revenue accounts and misstated accounts receivable in a direct manipulation of the revenue accounts' [AP]. Improper cutoff is a separate item in the Ch 8.7 inventory-manipulation list (deep 263), not tied to HealthSouth.
findings.fix: correct: false revenue and misstated receivables (HealthSouth in Ch 8.7)

findings.claim: The two are linked: managerial decisions affect what financial accounting must report.
findings.failure_mode: linkage direction not in deep or source
findings.evidence: Deep 25 gives the two definitions only. Source 1196 (Ch 1.1): 'Financial accounting is also a foundation for understanding managerial accounting'; source 1223-1224: management 'would use both financial and managerial accounting information to help improve the business'. Neither says managerial decisions shape what financial accounting must report.
findings.fix: correct: The two are linked: financial accounting is a foundation for managerial accounting, and management uses both to improve the business (Ch 1.1). cycle-to-deep: 'Financial accounting is also a foundation for understanding managerial accounting' (Ch 1.1)

findings.claim: The book takes the position that "the accrual method is theoretically preferable to the cash basis of accounting"

findings.claim: each materially affects reported income and AR. The text's position is that auditors are the discipline.
findings.failure_mode: loosened: 'materially' added; auditors' acceptance check upgraded to 'the discipline'
findings.evidence: Deep 307: each choice is within GAAP 'but each affecting reported income and AR balances'; the changes 'would need to be considered acceptable by the company's outside auditors during the annual independent audit' [V]. Deep 309: ratio analysis and trend analysis are the analyst's tools to spot earnings management.
findings.fix: correct: each affects reported income and AR. The text notes such changes would need to be accepted by the company's outside auditors in the annual audit, and presents ratio and trend analysis as the analyst's tools for spotting earnings management.

findings.claim: Replaces industry-specific revenue recognition with a principle-based approach affecting every revenue decision.
findings.failure_mode: hedge dropped; AICPA attribution dropped

findings.claim: The text takes a sharp position that "management teams typically fail to invest either time or attention into making or periodically revisiting and revising reasonably supportable estimates of asset lives or salvage values" [V]
findings.failure_mode: marker wrong: borrowed words marked [V] and presented as the text's own position
findings.evidence: Source 29630-29637 (Ch 11.3): the sentence is in quotation marks with footnote 7, Howard B. Levy, 'Depreciable Asset Lives,' The CPA Journal (2016). Deep 378 marks it [V, citing The CPA Journal]. The text's own position is the next sentence: 'This failure is not an ethical approach to properly accounting for the use of assets.'
findings.fix: re-mark: [BT]; correct: The text quotes The CPA Journal that "management teams typically fail to invest either time or attention into making or periodically revisiting and revising reasonably supportable estimates of asset lives or salvage values" [BT], and calls this failure not an ethical approach.

findings.claim: US GAAP probable threshold is ~80%; IFRS uses ~50%
findings.failure_mode: practitioner rule of thumb stated as the standard's threshold
findings.evidence: Deep 432: US GAAP probable 'often interpreted at ~80% likelihood'. Source 32025-32028 (Ch 12.3): probable 'is often assessed as an 80% likelihood by practitioners'; IFRS 'more likely than not' is 'typically assessed at 50% by practitioners'.
findings.fix: correct: Practitioners often assess US GAAP 'probable' at about 80% likelihood; IFRS defines probable as "more likely than not" [BT], typically assessed at about 50%.

findings.fix: cycle-to-deep: add the Ch 10.1 consistency-principle passage (source 26917-26923) to Part X

findings.claim: Earnings management within GAAP is legal; earnings manipulation outside GAAP is fraud.
findings.failure_mode: hedge dropped: manipulation equated with fraud
findings.evidence: Deep 307 [V]: earnings manipulation 'typically ignores GAAP rules to alter earnings significantly. Carried to an extreme, manipulation can lead to fraudulent behavior'. Key Concept 4 in this distillation states it correctly ('can shade into fraud').
findings.fix: correct: Earnings management works within GAAP; earnings manipulation typically ignores GAAP rules and, carried to an extreme, can lead to fraud.

findings.claim: Most of the load-bearing chapters present three or four (cost-flow, depreciation, bad-debt allowance, revenue recognition for long-term work).
findings.failure_mode: count wrong for one listed item
findings.evidence: Deep 313-316: two methods for long-term contracts (percentage of completion, completed contract), plus the installment method for real estate (deep 318). Four cost-flow assumptions (deep 328-333), three depreciation methods (deep 372-376), three allowance methods (deep 290-294).
findings.fix: correct: Most of the load-bearing chapters present two to four (four cost-flow assumptions, three depreciation methods, three allowance methods, two long-term-contract revenue methods).

findings.claim: What would the external auditor say if asked to defend the choice in an SOX 302 review?
findings.failure_mode: SOX section attached to the wrong party
findings.evidence: Deep 240: Section 302 is the CEO and CFO's personal certification. The auditor's SOX duty is the internal control report (deep 235); auditor acceptance of estimate changes happens 'during the annual independent audit' (deep 307).
findings.fix: correct: What would the external auditor say about the choice in the annual audit? If the auditor would push back, that is a signal worth attending to before the CEO and CFO certify under SOX 302.

findings.claim: Switching methods requires explicit disclosure and justification under full disclosure.
findings.failure_mode: rule in source but not in deep; tied to the wrong principle
findings.evidence: Deep 89 gives full disclosure only in general terms. Source 26919-26923 (Ch 10.1) ties method change to the consistency principle: a change is allowed 'if the company finds that a different method more accurately reflects results of operations, but the change requires disclosure in the company's notes'.
findings.fix: correct: Switching is allowed where a different method more accurately reflects results, but the change requires note disclosure (consistency principle, Ch 10.1). cycle-to-deep: add source 26917-26923 to Part X

findings.claim: Follow-up: test whether costs meet capitalisation criteria (extending useful life, increasing capacity), not merely 'necessary to the business'.
findings.failure_mode: subsequent-expenditure test presented as the whole capitalisation criterion
findings.evidence: Deep 368: capitalised cost includes 'all of the costs necessary to place the asset into service'; the extend-life / increase-capacity test separates later improvements from routine repairs and maintenance, which are expensed.
findings.fix: correct: Follow-up: test acquisition costs against 'necessary to place the asset into service' and later costs against whether they extend useful life or increase capacity; routine repairs and maintenance are expensed (Ch 11.2-11.3).

findings.claim: under SOX, certain non-audit services are prohibited

findings.claim: The capitalisation criterion (extending useful life or increasing capacity) is narrow; 'necessary to operations' is broad and not the criterion.

findings.evidence: Deep 368: capitalised cost includes 'all of the costs necessary to place the asset into service'; the extend-life / increase-capacity test applies to later expenditures.

notes: Faithful core: GAAP principles list, cost-flow and IFRS/LIFO passage (both [V] fragments verbatim at source 26888-26889), bad-debt methods, contingent-liability matrix, fraud triangle, auditor independence, case figures (BMS $150M/$1.5B, Enron $40B, Waste Management $1.7B). Integration rows for Organizational Behavior (six-step process, six barriers, reflective/reactive, programmed/non-programmed at OB deep 173-192) and Accounting Vol 2 check out; Business Ethics row is sound except the front-page claim. The worked example is where drift concentrates: it leans on accounting knowledge from outside the source (matching-supports-LIFO, cumulative-effect adjustment, LIFO reserve) and claims the front-page test as a source concept. Three source-supported gaps in the deep ref worth cycling: the consistency principle and method-change note disclosure (Ch 10.1, source 26917-26923), the IRS LIFO conformity exception (source 26924-26927), and materiality (Ch 8.4, source 22187-22189). Deep ref 74 misquotes the accrual passage ('method' for 'basis of accounting'). Structural: the distillation carries no verbatim blockquotes (open-nc sources call for 2-5), and the integration table mixes non-corpus frameworks (FASB SFAC 6, COSO, SOX, Cressey, IFRS) in with corpus references. 'Bernie Madoff's Ponzi scheme' follows deep 699; the source (21401) says Madoff 'swindled' tens of billions and never uses 'Ponzi'.
